en: The Entrance to Yoga. Homage to Tārā!
Having heard the noble treatise and having ascertained the ultimate reality, [one enters].
Seated upon a soft cushion, the practitioner, endowed with faith, should commence yoga. // 1 //

Having thoroughly understood the manifold web of conceptual constructions—that both the grasped and the grasper, neither one, nor both, am I alone, immersed in nirvāṇa—there is the meditative attainment of the mind. // 2 //
Having perceived the entirety of the knowable as nothing but the luminous yoga, one should enter the body with the vajra of the knowledge of suchness. (3)
Free from all modes of appearance, devoid of the distinction between beginning and end, and non-conceptual, everything becomes like the sky, pierced by the rays of a thousand suns. // 4 //
One perceives one's own mind as being nothing but its own appearance, primordially unarisen;
and that by which one perceives this is likewise observed in the same way. // 5 //
That non-apprehension is non-thought (*acitta*), the knowledge of suchness (*tathatājñāna*), and its limit (*tatkoṭi*).
Thus, through the practice of darkness, one attains the cessation of what is felt by wisdom (*prajñāveditanirodha*). // 6 //
Endowed with these, the yogi accomplishes the welfare of sentient beings in manifold ways;
once this is perfected, the yogi abides forever upon the noble path. // 7 //
...and having rendered it unshakable by the Māras of the afflictions and others, he always applies himself to the Perfection of Wisdom therein. // 8 //
Many others, such as meditative absorption, yoga, generosity, passion, and so forth, are accomplished. // 9 //
The Introduction to Yoga is completed.
This is the work of the venerable Ārya-Dignāga.
